**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup while you're in college. If your side project takes off on its own, he'd say it's reasonable to run with it, and then you have to choose between that and being a student.

He thinks a startup takes over your life, so you can't really do both. He also thinks you lose nothing by waiting, because you're more likely to succeed later.

**Based on:** said it. The 2014 answer was given to students, and the 2026 essay keeps the same rule.

**Why he'd say it**
- The rule, plainly stated: "Do not start a startup in college." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 18:56, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)
- Why it doesn't fit with school: "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 18:22)
- You give up nothing by waiting: "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12)
- Your early twenties are for open-ended exploration that success would take away. He says to "plunge deeply into projects on a whim that seem like they have no payoff" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 19:32). Of Facebook, he says "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 20:40).
- He still holds this in 2026: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]], https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)

**Your side project**
- Your question is really about the exception. He says the best startup ideas begin as side projects: "None of these companies were even supposed to be companies at first, they were all just side projects." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 25:08)
- If a project takes off, "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12)
- In 2026 he puts more weight on that exception. He says Microsoft and Meta both "got started during reading period at Harvard", and that a significant number of student side projects "would be incipient startups". About the student whose project takes off, he asks: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]])
- So build the project for fun, in your free time. Don't enroll in "startup mode" in advance. The sign is traction: if users want it and it grows, you'd be choosing between the project and the degree. That is the point where he'd say running with it is reasonable.

**What he'd tell you to do now**
- "Just learn." He reduces his advice for young would-be founders to those two words ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 30:49).
- Keep the project for something you and your friends want. He says "usually young founders should make something that they themselves want. You don't have enough experience yet to know what other people need." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]])

**What would change his answer:** real traction that you can't serve part-time. He'd say that's when you run with it.

**Caveats**
- His advice is a bit inconsistent. In the same 2014 talk he says "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it", which sits awkwardly with waiting ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 33:36). Both the vault and I read this as a shift in emphasis, not a reversal.
- The 2026 essay is addressed to universities, not to students. It doesn't say outright what a student should do.
- He's YC's founder, so he has a stake in the model of "finish school, then apply to YC". The vault flags this in [[profile]].

**Verdict:** Yes, Paul Graham thinks you should go to Silicon Valley, but "for a bit" is enough, and he wants you to come back. He gave this answer to a Stockholm audience, so it was aimed at people in your position.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high)

**Why he'd say it**
- He treats it as a settled answer: "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 0:36, [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s))
- **Peers:** "You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." (@ 1:09)
- **Serendipity:** "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." (@ 3:20)
- **Speed:** "Things also tend to move faster in the big centers because the people are better, they're more confident, and that's more decisive." (@ 3:53) Investors there decide faster because competition punishes waiting. He also says that investors outside the Valley "implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate", and that "if you leave for Silicon Valley, you make this rule operate in reverse." (@ 6:39)
- **The effect on you:** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." (@ 8:19) Up close, "it no longer seems an impossible goal, just a hard one." (@ 10:34)
- **Culture:** "In Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason." (@ 12:15)

**Coming back:** He frames returning as a duty to your city: "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." (@ 16:10) He thinks the Valley's money, culture and better startups come home with you. He also says the "Silicon Valley of Europe" job "is still up for grabs." (@ 20:04)

**What they've done:** He invested in a couple of companies started by people he knows in England, though he doesn't usually invest outside YC. One of them moved to Silicon Valley. (@ 12:47)

**What would change his answer / caveats**
- **He's talking his own book.** He says so himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point." (@ 17:16) His recommended way to do it is YC: "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." (@ 17:16) YC makes money from the founders he's telling to come.
- **The data is soft.** He says YC startups that go home are "only about half as likely to become unicorns" (@ 18:57), then discounts it as selection bias: it also measures the founders' "confidence and the determination". The figure is YC's own and comes with no method.
- **Family can outweigh it.** "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company." (@ 19:30)
- **Other YC voices are softer.** Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees that YC's rule to move to San Francisco was right, but he says he has "less of an intuition for it now". That's a weaker endorsement than PG's flat yes ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]]).

I'd flag one gap: the vault has nothing from PG on whether a Stockholm startup with real traction and good investor access still needs the move. His case rests on peers, speed and investor respect. If you already have those, his own reasoning says the move matters less. That's my inference, not something he said.

**Verdict:** Stop polishing the deck and stop chasing more meetings. Spend the time making the company something investors chase. Seibel says that is the only version of fundraising that works: you need a company growing so well that you could walk away from any deal.

He doesn't see the months you've spent as progress. He sees them as the costly part: "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)). That comes from a failed raise of his own, described below.

**Based on:** said it, from one October 2026 episode with Dalton Caldwell, backed by Paul Graham's older and consistent view.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Most investors chase deals. They don't wait for pitches.** Seibel asked investors who now want to invest what share of their deals they chase versus what share come in the front door. "The answers I got only varied between 8020 chase and 9010 chase." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:03, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s)). So a deck and a run of follow-ups work against the odds. Making the company something investors chase works with them: "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds."
- **Traction beats the deck.** When Socialcam was "the number two app in the app store," their deck "kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us," plus stats going up and to the right ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 9:30, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s)). Caldwell, his co-host, adds that it's "way better to be like a very bad fundraiser ... with something that's working than someone that's a very good fundraiser with ... something that's not working at all." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 5:35). Caldwell credits the idea to Paul Graham, whose own 2014 version is: "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 9:51)
- **Founder time belongs on the company.** In his Startup School talk, Seibel said "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([[yt-1hHMwLxN6EM]] @ 11:11, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s)). This is the same rule he applies to MVPs.
- **Leverage is your ability to walk away.** In YC office hours, founders asked how to raise a good round or what belongs in a pitch deck. Seibel and Caldwell would reply, "how much leverage do you have?" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 1:06). The answer mattered more than a better deck or a better process. The wiki summary of the episode says the more badly you need a deal, the less leverage you have. Caldwell's version: "the definition of leverage in this situation is that if any deal dies how much do you care" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 13:23). If you take follow-up meeting after follow-up meeting hoping one converts, you're in the position of needing the deal.
- **Months of meetings can hurt you.** In the episode they describe investors who keep meeting founders for months "in case" the company takes off, and say those meetings make takeoff less likely. The wiki's summary of that passage doesn't attribute it to either host, so treat it as the pair's view. Seibel does say he is "so not aligned" with "gaslight[ing] them into thinking you're going to invest" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 9:30).

**What he's done:** Justin.tv spent about eight months trying to raise. With two months of runway left and the money clearly not coming, the team tried to make the company profitable. Seibel says they got more done in those two months than in the months of pitching ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44). The line he quotes from that time: "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die."

**What he'd tell you to do now**
1. Treat the months of pitching as a signal that you lack leverage. Don't treat it as a pitch-quality problem.
2. Pause the process and spend the time on growth, users or revenue. Come back when you can show a graph that goes up and to the right.
3. Don't depend on any single investor or deal. His sales rule is "you can't need any one deal" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 11:43).

**What would change his answer:** Nothing in the vault covers raising on a thesis or team alone, with no traction. Everything above assumes you can still move the traction. If the product is already growing and investors are still stalling, his logic points the other way. You'd have leverage, so you'd run a short, tight process and leave anyone who strings you along.

**Caveats on the source:** The episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, the fund Caldwell co-founded, so the advice about respecting founders' time also serves their own business. They also joke that VCs wouldn't like them saying this ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:37). The "chase" statistic is an informal poll of investors Seibel asked, not data.

My own view, since you asked what he'd say: his case is strongest when traction can still be built. It's weaker for deep-tech or pre-product companies, where traction can't come first. I can't tell from your message which one you are.

**Verdict:** Stop the letter-trading. Call your cofounder directly, agree on a no-fault split, and have them give back most of their vested stock. At 9 months, Seibel's number is about 1–2% or less, with reasonable severance and clean paperwork. Settle it in about a week for roughly $2,000.

**Based on:** said it. Seibel addressed a pre-PMF breakup where the leaver is vested and wants to keep the stock. The numbers apply directly, so confidence is high on the direction and medium on the exact percentage.

**Why he'd say it**
- Before PMF the stock is nearly worthless, so a legal fight is really a fight over ego. "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 11:36, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s))
- Lawyers profit from the conflict itself. "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." (@ 12:07, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=727s)) And: "Don't get fooled by service providers. Don't spend a lot of money." (@ 20:50)
- Vested stock doesn't change this, because the leaver is cashing in a hedge while you carry the risk. "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." (@ 14:47) "Like, you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." (@ 15:21)
- Seibel's number: "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." (@ 18:39) He repeats it later: "Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." (@ 21:22, high confidence)
- His recipe is "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out" (@ 18:39). He says "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000."

**How to run it**
1. **Move fast.** "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." (@ 9:26) If it's the company that's over, not just the partnership, the equity question mostly disappears, and shutting down cleanly is the same logic. That second step is my extension, not something he said about this case.
2. **Be the generous, responsible party.** "it is so cheap to be nice," and "everyone in your company is looking at you right now." (@ 17:33) Seibel says acting responsible "often... [doesn't] trigger victimness on the other side, too." (@ 18:06)
3. **Don't litigate who was at fault.** Caldwell, Seibel's co-host, says the right frame is "no fault from both sides" and "Don't try to ruin the other person. Don't try to ruin the reputation." (@ 13:42) Seibel adds: "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." (@ 21:54)
4. **If you need a mediator, don't make them the judge.** (@ 19:46)
5. **Remember it's a long game.** Caldwell: "being known as the super litigious scorched earth person, you're never going to work again." (@ 16:28) And if you handle it well, "this is a non-mortal wound." (@ 20:18)

**What would change his answer**
- **Misconduct.** "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." (@ 21:54)
- **The company has real value.** His advice is explicitly for pre-PMF companies where the stock is worth little. If you're sitting on a funded round or real revenue, the numbers change.
- **Where you stand.** I don't know whether you're the one staying or leaving. His percentages are written for the founder who stays. If you're the leaver, his logic still says a low number is the norm, but you'd be negotiating against it.

**Caveats**
- This episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, where Caldwell is a partner. The advice leans toward the founder who stays and the cap table, which is an investor's lens ([[profile]]).
- Seibel's numbers are norms, not entitlements. If your cofounder's stock is vested under your agreement, they can legally refuse, and your lawyers are probably telling you that. I'd still take his advice on cost and speed, but that's my read, not his. I haven't checked how your vesting schedule or cliff works, so ask your lawyer that one question.

**Correction first:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, in the vault's only source for it, and he was talking about Tan. The vault has no statement from Tan on a YC premium or on a gap with second place.

Altman was a guest at YC's Startup School (July 2026), with Tan hosting. He said: "I also think that I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded." ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56, [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)). He said "Gary probably can't" because Tan runs YC and would be bragging about his own product.

**Verdict:** Altman's reason is network effects. He says the growing gap "is a reminder of the power of network effects" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56).

**Based on:** said it, though only briefly. Altman gives the network-effects reason in one sentence and doesn't spell out the mechanism.

**Why he'd say it**
- The thing YC offers is meeting your future co-founders and peers. He says YC's old limiter was "figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem," because talented people "couldn't find their tribe" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:25).
- YC's old advice to move to San Francisco "used to be very heretical... And looking back, it was clearly right," because in the Bay Area "magic happened. You got a lot of like lucky chances and collisions" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:25–16:56).
- His next point is to get into networks early: "finding networks that you can be part of... help you just meet those people," because "it takes a long time to compound" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 17:28–18:02). Networks gain value as more people join, so the biggest one pulls further ahead of the rest.
- Tan adds that "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 23:35). That is the closest Tan comes in the vault, and it isn't a claim about a premium.

**Caveats**
- Altman hedges on the Bay Area itself: "I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now." The vault's page on this source notes that the claim comes from YC's former president, speaking at YC's own event ([[hiring/cofounders/finding-cofounders-and-your-people]]).
- He gives no figures or evidence that the gap has grown. It is his judgment.

**Related in the vault:** [[startups/strategy/inducing-network-effects]] (PG says YC itself turned out to have network effects) and [[fundraising/investors/what-does-a-yc-batch-give-founders]].

The vault doesn't back this up, so I'm answering from what it does say.

**Verdict:** Livingston never said that. What she said is nearly the opposite. She called herself "soft and sensitive" next to the "hardened and aggressive" and "ruthless" investors of the time, and she says she screened for earnest founders, not ruthless ones.

**Based on:** said it (the premise is contradicted by her own words)

**Where the "ruthless" line comes from**
- In her 2018 talk she describes her own role at YC: "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s; by: livingston; auto-captions). The word "ruthless" describes some investors she knew, not founders. She says she contrasted with them by caring "how founders were feeling" and by counselling them through overwhelm and co-founder disputes.

**What she looked for**
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s).
- She asked "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" (same source, @ 14:51).
- She declined applicants she could tell were conceited. She says "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" (@ 15:27). She admits YC has funded some conceited founders since.
- In 2024 she added "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 45:34).

**The toughness she did value**
- She is for boldness and persistence: "you do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45).
- She wants independent-minded founders: "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 51:09).
- Determination is on her list ("they're all very determined", @ 51:43). She doesn't tie any of this to aggression or winning.

**What the vault attributes to others**
- Any "tough founders win" idea comes from PG, not her. In 2014 he said the hardest part of judging founders was predicting how tough and ambitious they would become. In 2026 he said YC wants "formidable" founders, meaning people who get what they want in any situation ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 9:57). See [[founders/traits/what-makes-a-founder-formidable]]. Even there, formidable isn't the same as ruthless.

**What would change this answer:** a source I haven't found where she endorses aggressive or ruthless founders. I searched the wiki and raw transcripts for "ruthless", "aggressive" and related terms and found nothing like that. The vault only holds two long Livingston sources, so a remark in an interview outside the vault is possible.
